Currently, there are three officially supported scenarios/configurations.
Usages outside of these scenarios are not guaranteed to work, but please
feel free to file bug reports documenting your experience and any issues
you encountered to help expand support.

#### Browser Applications (Manual Boot)

The setup is largely similar to how Ember works out-of-the-box. Normally,
Ember will boot a default instance for your Application on "DOM ready".
However, you can customize this behavior by disabling

.

For example, this allows you to render a miniture demo of your application
into a specific area on your marketing website:

Or perhaps you might want to boot two instances of your app on the same
page for a split-screen multiplayer experience:

Do note that each app instance maintains their own registry/container, so
they will run in complete isolation by default.

#### Server-Side Rendering (also known as FastBoot)

This setup allows you to run your Ember app in a server environment using
Node.js and render its content into static HTML for SEO purposes.
In this scenario, because Ember does not have access to a global

object in the Node.js environment, you must provide one explicitly. In practice,
in the non-browser environment, the stand-in

object only needs to
implement a limited subset of the full DOM API. The

library is known
to work.

Since there is no DOM access in the non-browser environment, you must also
specify a DOM

option
(as opposed to a selector string like

for details.

#### Server-Side Resource Discovery

This setup allows you to run the routing layer of your Ember app in a server
environment using Node.js and completely disable rendering. This allows you
to simulate and discover the resources (i.e. AJAX requests) needed to fulfill
a given request and eagerly "push" these resources to the client.
